About this Group Meeting
MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
Denolle Lab research-group pilot
Thirteen one-hour meetings, taken one at a time

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
Purpose
Reconstruct how experimental, observational, historical, and theoretical research actually proceeds, then translate those lessons into scientifically grounded agent designs and evaluations. The adequacy of a hypothesis-generation/testing loop is a question to investigate, not a conclusion the seminar assumes.
One proposal runs alongside the rest: that agents for science let a researcher work competently across more fields, making individual polymathy practical again. It is an open question here. Meeting 11 states the hypothesis, the historical evidence bearing on it, and the observations that would count against it.
Start with the glossary. It gives working definitions of the modes of inquiry and of the terms the quarter measures, field-shaping, novelty, depth, interdisciplinarity, and impact, and meeting 1 revises it. This is an exploratory quarter for the group. Nothing here is a settled syllabus, and the bibliography is meant to grow. How to contribute covers adding a note, a reading, or a correction.

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
How the paper pairings work
Each meeting uses two scholarly papers with a specific relationship: argument/counterpoint, discovery/diagnostic scrutiny, capability/calibration, or practice/framework. A pairing is not necessarily a disagreement. Read the assigned portions; rotating discussants read both in depth. No participant is expected to read every optional extension.
Meetings 1, 6, 9, and 13 also carry discussant-led papers: the full-length version of Cleland’s argument in meeting 1, Ioannidis on false findings in meeting 6, Geller on earthquake prediction in meeting 9, and the two critiques in meeting 13, which merges what were previously separate architecture and evaluation meetings. Each is taken in depth by one rotating discussant; everyone else reads the abstract. The reading load stays at two papers per participant throughout.
For each paper distinguish its scientific claim, the evidence offered, its limits, and the evidence it provides about the research process. A philosophical argument, a retrospective autobiography, an archival history, a primary research report, and a benchmark paper are not interchangeable records of actual practice. Where chronology is not documented, label reconstruction as inference.

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
Standing questions

What was known at the beginning, and what was the initial question?
Which observation, representation, instrument, or model changed the next action?
When did the eventual hypothesis appear, and what was exploratory or confirmatory?
Where did surprise, failed expectation, opportunism, or missing evidence matter?
What is documented about the trajectory, and what disappears from the publication narrative?
Which action could an agent perform, and how would we know it had performed it well?

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
Quarter outputs
The group develops an inquiry-action vocabulary, exploration policy, trace-inference worksheet, measurement-provenance checklist, adaptive observation plan, Novelty Dossier, Polymathy Profile, Scientific Advance Profile, and finally an agent architecture and evaluation protocol produced together. Across meetings 1 to 9 it also keeps an inquiry-mode ledger, one row per reconstructed episode, so that the question of where a hypothesis gate would have helped is answered case by case rather than by impression. In parallel it can run the corpus study, which codes the mode of inquiry of published papers with the glossary as codebook and relates mode to impact, novelty, interdisciplinarity, and depth, so that the nine hand-reconstructed cases have a counterpart at scale. The working rubrics are design proposals to revise, not validated scales.
Before specifying any agent, consult the prior art chapter: it catalogues the systems and benchmarks that already exist and, for each, what its scores do not establish. The point of building anything here is to add to that record rather than repeat it.

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
Reading access and public use
Every assigned paper has a DOI, publisher, repository, or official proceedings link. Some full texts require institutional access. This book does not redistribute journal PDFs or claim that freely readable papers may automatically be republished. Use the publisher’s download link or institutional library for personal reading, and check the license before putting third-party files on the public site.
The bibliography collects every reading by meeting, with links and access notes, the readings the group adds during the quarter, and the full reference list generated from a reusable BibTeX file.

Current evidence does not establish that one architecture is best for all scientific inquiry.

title: Glossary: modes of inquiry and terms of assessment
text:
How to use a mode
These are the working definitions the seminar uses. The modes of inquiry are the rows of the inquiry-mode ledger and the codebook for the corpus study. The terms of assessment are the variables meetings 10 to 12 measure. Meeting 1 revises this page, and the revised page is the seminar’s first output, the inquiry-action vocabulary. Every definition is tied to the readings that motivate it, and every mode has three coding aids: how to recognize it in a paper, what evidence it produces, and how it characteristically fails.
Every citation links to its full record in the bibliography. Nothing here is settled. A definition that fails on a paper someone in the group has written is a definition to fix, and the page records the fix.
A mode of inquiry is characterized by its epistemic function, what the work does for knowledge, and by its decisive move, the action that changes what comes next. Papers mix modes; a single study can describe, then explore, then form a hypothesis, then test it (Cleland 2002). For the ledger and the corpus study, code the decisive mode and record secondary modes separately. Code the mode the paper presents; where the trajectory is documented and differs from the presentation, record both, because the gap between them is what standing question 5 is about (Holmes 1987).
Three of the rows, instruments, methods, and replication, are also contribution roles in the Scientific Advance Profile. They are modes here because each has its own epistemic function: producing data that did not exist, extracting information from data that did, and testing what survives. Instruments and methods are kept apart by that line, new data against new information from existing data, and not by whether hardware is involved. Infrastructure is not a row. A seismic network, a catalog, a software package, and a standard are infrastructure for different modes, so the ledger and the corpus study record “shared infrastructure” as a flag on any row. An automated system (King et al. 2009; Boiko et al. 2023) is not a mode of its own either: it is a method that performs some mode, and the coding question is which.

title: Glossary: modes of inquiry and terms of assessment
text:
Coding rules










Mode
Recognize it by
Evidence it produces
Characteristic failure
Readings




Observation and description
A catalog, map, time series, or survey is the contribution; claims are about where, how often, and how large; no causal test
Coverage, completeness, and consistency of the record; reproducible by re-observation
Detection thresholds and coverage read as phenomena; the survey as an end in itself, Platt’s “eternal surveyor”
Powell (2007); Becker et al. (2019); Kuklick and Kohler (1996); Atwater (1987); Platt (1964)


Exploratory discovery
No hypothesis stated before the result; patterns then explanations; open-ended or unsupervised methods; a change of question mid-study
A pattern that reproduces in data not used to find it; an anomaly that explains more than the original question did
Forking paths, and a pattern found after inspection reported as a prediction; anomalies called error and dropped, which is the base rate
Steinle (1997); Karaca (2013); Franklin (2005); Tukey (1962); Bergen et al. (2019); Rouet-Leduc et al. (2017); Moore (2025); Yaqub (2018); Kuhn (1962); Fugelsang et al. (2004); Ioannidis (2005)


Hypothesis testing
Alternatives named before the outcome; a prediction that could have failed; controls, or a discriminating observable
The discriminating outcome, repeatable where the system allows manipulation; a trace that separates rivals where it does not
Auxiliary assumptions absorb the refutation; controls fixed before any data are the wrong controls; a test no outcome could fail
Platt (1964); Chamberlin (1965); Cleland (2001); Cleland (2002); Sykes (1967); Bakun and Lindh (1985); Bakun et al. (2005); Geller (1997); Schorlemmer et al. (2018)


Theory and mechanistic modeling
The derivation precedes the observation; a new object or concept; previously separate facts unified
Consequences later found where predicted; unification of independent evidence
A theory that predicts everything and so predicts nothing; a correct synthesis rejected on method; syntheses that, as Platt concedes, stand outside any method
Wilson (1965); Vine and Matthews (1963); Oreskes (1988); Platt (1964); Cleland (2002)


Simulation and prediction
Numerical models, ensembles, scenarios, forecasts, parameter estimation, misfit, equifinality
Skill on held-out observables; agreement across structurally different models; prospective tests
Fit mistaken for truth; simulation mistaken for experiment; validation claimed for an open system
Oreskes et al. (1994); Beven and Freer (2001); Tarantola (2006); Kirchner (2006); Schorlemmer et al. (2018); Rainforth et al. (2024)


Instruments and observing systems
The sensor, platform, or network is the contribution; results framed as what can now be seen; new data
Calibration and instrument response; the same signal on an independent sensor
A feature of the measurement chain taken for a feature of the world; the researcher of one instrument
Lindsey et al. (2019); Lindsey et al. (2020); Kuhn (1961); Tal (2013); Platt (1964)


Methods and computation
The algorithm, inversion, model code, or software is the contribution; results framed as what can now be computed or recovered from existing data
Synthetic tests and recovery of known signals; benchmarks against independent methods; adoption by others
A feature of the method taken for a feature of the world, such as a regularization artifact; leakage between development and test data; a loop that scores itself
Shapiro and Campillo (2004); Shapiro et al. (2005); Bergen et al. (2019); Kapoor and Narayanan (2023); Langley (1981); Kulkarni and Simon (1988); King et al. (2009); Boiko et al. (2023); Szymanski et al. (2023); Leeman et al. (2024)


Synthesis and reconstruction
No new intervention; several evidence types; a past event or a system reconstructed; reviews, meta-analyses, and connections between literatures
Convergence of independent traces; a discriminating trace, Cleland’s smoking gun; a connection later confirmed by measurement
Traces attenuated or misread; false connections between literatures; retellings replacing primary sources
Cleland (2001); Cleland (2002); Atwater (1987); Nelson et al. (1996); Satake et al. (1996); Yamaguchi et al. (1997); Swanson (1986); Sourati and Evans (2023)


Replication and validation
A known result re-obtained or moved to a new region, period, or instrument; a benchmark; a calibration study
The result survives, or fails in an informative way
Devalued as unoriginal; leakage between development and test data; a benchmark that measures the wrong construct
Lindsey et al. (2020); Nosek et al. (2018); Schorlemmer et al. (2018); Kapoor and Narayanan (2023); Flake and Fried (2020); Messick (1995); Chen et al. (2025)


Use-inspired and co-produced research
An application partner or a decision the work informs; products such as maps, forecasts, and services; standards and guidelines as outputs
The product is used, and its use is checked against outcomes; salience, credibility, and legitimacy to the users
Usefulness mistaken for truth, or truth for usefulness; the user’s question narrowing the science; use measured by citations, which miss it
Stokes (1997); Cash et al. (2003); Jordan et al. (2011); Becker et al. (2019); Bornmann and Daniel (2008)




Sub-modes
The readings distinguish finer kinds of inquiry within several rows. Record the sub-mode where it is clear; it is what the ledger’s “decisive move” column will often name.

Under exploratory discovery: exploratory experimentation, the systematic variation of conditions without a stable hypothesis (Steinle 1997); exploratory data analysis, looking at data to find structure and questions (Tukey 1962); and serendipity, an unexpected observation recognized as worth following (Yaqub 2018).
Under hypothesis testing: the controlled experiment, in which the investigator produces the test condition (Cleland 2002); the discriminating observation, a test on data the system does not allow one to manipulate (Sykes 1967); and the smoking gun, a trace that picks one hypothesis out of a stated set (Cleland 2001).
Under theory and mechanistic modeling: conceptual synthesis, a new object that reorganizes old observations (Wilson 1965); and theory-led prediction, a derived quantity then sought (Vine and Matthews 1963).
Under instruments and observing systems: instrument-led observation, where the questions follow the sensor (Lindsey et al. 2019).
Under methods and computation: methods that create a new observable from data everyone already had, as ambient-noise interferometry did with seismic noise (Shapiro and Campillo 2004; Shapiro et al. 2005); and automated discovery, a system that performs generation, selection, or execution (Langley 1981; Kulkarni and Simon 1988), which is coded here even when it drives a laboratory, because what it adds is the computation.
Under synthesis and reconstruction: trace inference, explaining present traces by past events that cannot be rerun (Cleland 2002); and literature-based synthesis, new claims from connecting published results (Swanson 1986).

title: Glossary: modes of inquiry and terms of assessment
text:
Terms of assessment
Meeting 1 fixes a first working definition for each of these, so that meetings 10 to 12 and the corpus study measure variables defined before the data are seen rather than after. Each entry gives the working definition, the measures the literature uses, and what those measures do not capture.
Novelty. Newness of a specific claim relative to a stated corpus and time. It is not correctness and not importance (Uzzi et al. 2013; Fontana et al. 2020). Measures: atypical combinations of cited references (Uzzi et al. 2013), distance of a paper’s words from the prior literature (Shibayama et al. 2021), and expert judgment, which disagrees with itself (Boudreau et al. 2016). Not captured: whether the claim is true, and what the searched corpus missed. The seminar’s rule is “no precedent located within this search,” never “never done before.” See meeting 10.
Depth. Concentration of a researcher’s or a paper’s competence within one area, the opposite of breadth. Measures: the concentration of an author’s publications across topics (Teodoridis 2018; Teodoridis et al. 2019; Rassenfosse et al. 2022), and for a paper, the concentration of its references in one field, which is the low end of the interdisciplinarity measure below. Not captured: depth is relative to how finely a field is divided, and the same researcher is deep by one taxonomy and broad by another.
Interdisciplinarity. Integration of knowledge from distinct fields in one piece of work, as opposed to work that merely draws on several (Wagner et al. 2011). Measures: the diversity of the fields a paper cites, counting how many fields, how evenly, and how distant they are from one another (Stirling 2007; Porter and Rafols 2009); the disciplines of the authors; and atypical reference pairs (Uzzi et al. 2013). Not captured: field taxonomies are conventions, and a diverse reference list shows what was read, not what was understood. Where such work lands is a measured question, taken up below and in meeting 11.
Impact. Downstream uptake or consequence of a contribution (Dellsén 2016). Measures: citations normalized by field and year, which makes counts comparable across fields (Radicchi et al. 2008; Waltman 2016); models of long-term citation from early history (Wang et al. 2013); and uptake that citations miss, such as reuse of data, software, and standards, and use in decisions, which is the whole of the use-inspired row above. Not captured: citations measure attention and convention as much as use (Bornmann and Daniel 2008), and they inflate over time (Petersen et al. 2025). Novelty is penalized at first and rewarded late (Wang et al. 2017).
Field-shaping. A contribution after which a field’s questions, methods, or reference set are different. Unlike novelty, it is retrospective: it is a fact about what the field did next. Measures: the disruption index, which asks whether later papers cite a work instead of its predecessors or together with them (Funk and Owen-Smith 2017; Wu et al. 2019), with the corrections its critics require (Petersen et al. 2025; Park et al. 2023); becoming canonical in a field that keeps citing it (Chu and Evans 2021); delayed recognition, the sleeping beauty (Ke et al. 2015); and the appearance of a new topic whose papers cite it. Not captured: each measure operationalizes something different, and the seminar reports a profile rather than a score. See meeting 12, whose working definitions of advance, innovation, and impact this entry defers to.
Hypothesis gate. A rule that the next action in an inquiry must be a test of a stated hypothesis. The ledger asks, for each reconstructed episode, whether such a rule would have helped, hurt, or not applied at the decisive move. It is the design choice the seminar is questioning, and its best defenders are in the reading (Platt 1964; Ioannidis 2005; King et al. 2009).
Decisive move. The action in an episode that changed what came next: a record, a pattern, a test, a concept, a computation, a capability, a convergence, a replication, or a question posed by a user. It is what the ledger codes, and it is inferred from the record, so its evidence basis is recorded beside it.
Trajectory and narrative. The trajectory is what was done, in order. The narrative is the published account. They differ (Holmes 1987), and the difference is not misconduct; but only the trajectory is evidence about how inquiry proceeds, and most of what the seminar reads is narrative. Every ledger row says which it rests on.

title: Glossary: modes of inquiry and terms of assessment
text:
Where interdisciplinary work lands
The measured answer so far, which the seminar tests against its own cases. Papers that combine an unusual pairing of references with a conventional core are cited more than either alone (Uzzi et al. 2013). Researchers who work across fields publish less and are cited more (Leahey et al. 2017). Generalists outperform specialists where a field is moving fast and underperform them where it is slow (Teodoridis et al. 2019). Specialization is rewarded persistently in at least one large field (Rassenfosse et al. 2022). And the tools that lower the cost of breadth have so far narrowed what fields ask, while widening what individuals produce (Hao et al. 2026; Doshi and Hauser 2024). None of this observed this group, and the corpus study is where the group would find out whether it holds in its own literature.

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
The paper pair
Every citation on this page links to its full record in the bibliography, which also lists this meeting’s readings with access notes.
Pairing type: Methodological ideal / evidential counterpoint.
Platt, J. R. (1964). Strong Inference. Science, 146(3642), 347–353. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347
Read Platt in full. Identify the role of alternative explanations and discriminating observations.
Cleland, C. E. (2001). Historical science, experimental science, and the scientific method. Geology, 29(11), 987–990. https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2
Read Cleland’s Geology paper in full. It makes the argument in four pages, for geologists; the discussant brings the rest.

Why these papers belong together
Platt offers a prescriptive strategy; Cleland analyzes differences between experimental interventions and reconstructing past events. Neither paper directly records this group’s daily research. Test both against an actual project rather than declaring one a complete scientific method. (Platt 1964; Cleland 2001)


Discussant-led paper
One rotating discussant takes the following in depth and brings its argument into the discussion; everyone else reads the abstract.
Cleland, C. E. (2002). Methodological and Epistemic Differences between Historical Science and Experimental Science. Philosophy of Science, 69(3), 474–496. https://doi.org/10.1086/342455
The full version of the Geology paper above: the time asymmetry that makes trace-hunting a rational strategy rather than a consolation prize, the “smoking gun”, and the reply to the charge that historical science is epistemically inferior. The discussant brings what the four-page version leaves out. (Cleland 2002)


Reading notes
The convenor’s notes from the two assigned papers, offered as a starting point rather than a summary of the discussion. They bear on discussion question 3 below, on whether the papers describe how ideas are generated or how claims are warranted, and the diagram is the loop the case exercise compares a real project against. Page numbers are the journals’ own.

Inference, deduction, and hypothesis generation
Deduction is not the opposite of inference. It is one kind of inference. Platt’s workflow embeds deductive reasoning inside a broader process of inductive inference.








Term
Definition
Role in strong inference




Inference
Any reasoned movement from premises or evidence to a conclusion.
The general category containing deduction, induction, and other forms of reasoning.


Deduction
Reasoning in which the conclusion must follow if the premises are true.
Derives a predicted observation from each hypothesis: if \(H_i\) and its auxiliary assumptions hold, then \(P_i\) should occur.


Inductive inference
Reasoning from observations to a broader but provisional conclusion. New evidence can revise it.
Uses the observed outcome to exclude, retain, or refine hypotheses. This is what Platt calls the branching logical tree (Platt 1964, 347).


Hypothesis generation
The creative proposal of possible explanations, sometimes called abduction.
Produces the alternatives at the beginning of each cycle. Platt says this step requires “intellectual inventions, which must be cleverly chosen” rather than a mechanical rule, and sends the reader to Pólya for how to make them (Platt 1964, 347).



The logic within one branch. For a candidate hypothesis \(H_i\), together with auxiliary assumptions \(A\):
\[H_i + A \Rightarrow P_i\]
This movement from hypothesis to prediction is deduction.
If the experiment instead produces \(\neg P_i\), then:
\[\neg P_i \Rightarrow \neg(H_i + A)\]
This is the basis of exclusion. Strictly speaking, the test has contradicted the combination of the hypothesis and its assumptions, not the hypothesis alone. Platt does not draw that distinction; Cleland makes it the center of her case against falsificationism, with the astronomers who kept Newton and rejected an auxiliary assumption to find Neptune as the example (Cleland 2001, 988).
The resulting revision of the hypothesis set is inductive inference:
\[\{H_1, H_2, H_3\} + \text{observed outcome} \Rightarrow \text{a smaller, provisionally preferred set}\]
Observing \(P_i\) does not deductively prove \(H_i\), because another hypothesis might also predict \(P_i\). Strong inference addresses this problem by seeking observations for which the competing hypotheses make different predictions.


Platt’s branching discipline: strong inference
Platt’s strong inference is a repeating process of generating alternatives, designing an observation that distinguishes them, excluding incompatible alternatives, and refining what remains (Platt 1964, 347).

Figure 1.1: Platt’s strong inference as a branching loop. Each cycle generates alternatives, deduces predictions that differ between them, runs the experiment, excludes what the outcome rules out, and refines what remains. The hypotheses are contrasted, never proved.






Exclusion means that an observed outcome is incompatible with a prediction required by one or more hypotheses. Those hypotheses are removed from the current candidate set. The hypothesis that remains has survived this test; it has not been proved true.

The ideal experiment is therefore not merely one that produces information. It is one for which the possible outcomes change which explanations remain viable.
Is it Baconian? Platt says so himself. He traces the “conditional inductive tree” to Bacon’s Novum Organum, with its “Instances of the Fingerpost” that mark where roads part and its rule that induction must proceed by “proper rejections and exclusions” (Platt 1964, 349), and he presents Chamberlin’s multiple working hypotheses as the second invention “needed to round out the Baconian scheme” (Platt 1964, 350; Chamberlin 1965). In today’s vocabulary the exclusion step is eliminative induction, and Platt quotes Popper for the claim that science advances only by disproofs (Platt 1964, 350). Two things in the diagram are not Baconian and not in Platt. The distinction between \(H_i\) and \(A\) above the exclusion arrow is Cleland’s (Cleland 2001, 988). And the box that generates \(H_1\), \(H_2\), \(H_3\) has no rule inside it; Platt concedes as much, and the seminar’s question is what happens there.

The paper pair

Why these papers belong together
Tukey makes room for data-driven inquiry. Nosek and colleagues argue for clearer evidential status through preregistration. This is a complementary pairing, not exploration versus legitimate science. (Tukey 1962; Nosek et al. 2018)

Ioannidis, J. P. A. (2005). Why Most Published Research Findings Are False. PLoS Medicine, 2(8), e124. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124

Optional extensions

Kuhn (1962): Historical Structure of Scientific Discovery. Science (1962). Kuhn on the discovery of oxygen: an anomaly is recognized only once the concepts let it be seen, so a discovery has a duration rather than a date. Read against Moore.
Fugelsang et al. (2004): Theory and data interactions of the scientific mind: Evidence from the molecular and the cognitive laboratory. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology (2004). Dunbar’s studies of live laboratory meetings: scientists first attribute an unexpected result to error and pursue it only after it replicates. The base rate for anomaly follow-up.
Copeland (2019): On serendipity in science: discovery at the intersection of chance and wisdom. Synthese (2019). What separates serendipity from luck: preparation and the capacity to recognize. Complements Yaqub’s taxonomy.
Rouet-Leduc et al. (2017): Machine Learning Predicts Laboratory Earthquakes. Geophysical Research Letters (2017). A supervised model found that continuous acoustic noise predicts time to failure in a laboratory fault, a signal nobody had hypothesized, later followed up in Cascadia. A recent geoscience case of exploration-first discovery. Read it with the same suspicion the meeting applies to Moore.
Schmidhuber (2010): Formal Theory of Creativity, Fun, and Intrinsic Motivation (1990–2010). IEEE Transactions on Autonomous Mental Development (2010). A formal definition of interesting: progress in compressing what has been observed. One candidate for what an exploring agent optimizes when it is not optimizing a hypothesis test.

title: Scientific novelty: new to whom, compared with what?
text:
Agent-design or evaluation output
Novelty Dossier v1: atomic claims, novelty types, closest prior art, attempted disconfirmation, search coverage, apparently new component, uncertainty, and separate correctness/value judgments. Track missed novelty, false novelty, prior-art recall, claim localization, calibration, and paraphrase robustness.

Preserve distinctions and avoid a false historical test
Separate empirical, methodological/instrumental, conceptual, explanatory/theoretical, recombinant, and question novelty. A novelty judgment is relative to a specified corpus and time. It is not a correctness or importance judgment.
Historical replay is a discussion exercise, not automatically a leakage-free benchmark. Restricting retrieved papers does not remove later discoveries from a model’s training. Stronger evaluation can use prospective held-out work or controlled cases, with explicit limits on what those tasks represent.

title: Scientific polymathy: breadth, specialization, and borrowed competence
text:
Central question
Meeting 11 of 13
Under what conditions does breadth across fields produce better science than depth in one, and does an agent that supplies competence a researcher does not hold change that answer or only relabel who is borrowing?
crumbs: 11  Scientific polymathy: breadth, specialization, and borrowed competence

title: Scientific polymathy: breadth, specialization, and borrowed competence
text:
The paper pair
Every citation on this page links to its full record in the bibliography, which also lists this meeting’s readings with access notes.
Pairing type: Historical retrospective / formal argument for specialization.
Burke, P. (2020). The Polymath: A Cultural History from Leonardo da Vinci to Susan Sontag. Yale University Press. https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300250022/the-polymath/
Read the chapters covering the age of specialization and Burke’s stages of retreat from the polymathic ideal. Ask what a prosopography of roughly five hundred recognized polymaths can and cannot establish: the sample is selected on success, so it does not tell us how often breadth failed.
Kitcher, P. (1990). The Division of Cognitive Labor. The Journal of Philosophy, 87(1), 5–22. https://doi.org/10.2307/2026796
Read the model and the assumptions it needs. Note the central result: a community can be better off when individuals do not all work on the most promising problem, which makes specialization a collective strategy rather than a loss of ambition.

Why these papers belong together
Burke narrates a decline; Kitcher argues that the division of cognitive labor is rational. The pairing asks whether “polymathy declined” and “specialization is optimal” are the same claim in two registers, or genuinely different claims that could come apart. Neither paper concerns agents, which is why they are useful here: they set the terms before the technology is introduced. An agent that supplies borrowed competence either adds a worker to Kitcher’s division or changes how much one worker can cover, and those two readings imply different things about what breadth is worth. (Burke 2020; Kitcher 1990)

title: Scientific polymathy: breadth, specialization, and borrowed competence
text:
Agent-design or evaluation output
Polymathy Profile v1: a competence inventory using the held / borrowed / trusted / absent categories, a list of substitution candidates, and for each candidate the verification that must exist before delegation is acceptable. Record which verifications the group can actually perform and which are currently aspirational.

The hypothesis under test
The group is investigating a specific proposal: that agents for science let a researcher operate competently across more fields, making individual polymathy practical again in an era Burke describes as inhospitable to it. Nothing here assumes it is true, and the evidence could go either way.
It predicts that assisted researchers ask and answer questions that cross field boundaries they previously did not cross, and that the resulting work survives scrutiny by specialists in those fields. It would be disconfirmed if assistance instead produces work that specialists judge superficial or wrong, if the range of questions narrows toward what the tools handle well, or if apparent breadth turns out to be unverified trust in outputs nobody in the group can check. Note that “the group felt more capable” is not evidence for the hypothesis; it is consistent with both outcomes.

Wright et al. (2025): What and Whose Knowledge? Measuring Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models. Open preprint. A measurement of how varied the claims in model outputs actually are, and the counterpoint to this session’s hypothesis: shared tools may narrow the accessible range of knowledge rather than widen it.
Rassenfosse et al. (2022): Scientific rewards for biomedical specialization are large and persistent. Open access. Present-day evidence on what breadth costs a career, against which Burke’s historical decline story can be tested.
Jones (2009): The Burden of Knowledge and the “Death of the Renaissance Man”: Is Innovation Getting Harder?. Review of Economic Studies (2009). The mechanism behind Burke’s decline: as knowledge accumulates, reaching a frontier takes longer, so individuals specialize and teams grow. If agents lower the cost of reaching a frontier, this is the model the session’s hypothesis is a prediction of.
Wuchty et al. (2007): The Increasing Dominance of Teams in Production of Knowledge. Science (2007). Across twenty million papers, teams replaced solo authors and now produce the most cited work. Measures what took the polymath’s place.
Stichweh (1992): The Sociology of Scientific Disciplines: On the Genesis and Stability of the Disciplinary Structure of Modern Science. Science in Context (1992). Dates disciplinary specialization to around 1800, not the twentieth century. A check on the historical premise.
Teodoridis (2018): Understanding Team Knowledge Production: The Interrelated Roles of Technology and Expertise. Management Science (2018). A natural experiment: when the Kinect made motion sensing cheap, researchers collaborated less with the specialists whose skill it replaced. The closest existing test of “a tool that supplies competence changes who you need”.
Teodoridis et al. (2019): Creativity at the Knowledge Frontier: The Impact of Specialization in Fast- and Slow-paced Domains. Administrative Science Quarterly (2019). Generalists outperform specialists in fast-moving fields and underperform them in slow ones. Predicts where agent-assisted breadth should pay and where it should not.
Leahey et al. (2017): Prominent but Less Productive: The Impact of Interdisciplinarity on Scientists’ Research. Administrative Science Quarterly (2017). Interdisciplinary researchers publish less and are cited more. The present-day cost and reward of breadth, measured.
Hao et al. (2026): Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists’ impact but contract science’s focus. Nature (2026). Across 41 million papers, scientists who use AI tools publish more and are cited more, and the fields they work in narrow. The disconfirming observation this session names, measured at scale, though for AI tools rather than agents.
Doshi and Hauser (2024): Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content. Science Advances (2024). A controlled experiment with the same shape: individual gain, collective narrowing.

Burke’s history, a formal model, a preprint measurement, and a bibliometric career study are four different kinds of evidence. None of them observed this group, and none of them tested an agent-assisted researcher.

Optional extensions

The extensions below are grouped by what they are evidence of.
Systems that predate language models. The lineage the prior art chapter now opens with.

Langley (1981): Data-Driven Discovery of Physical Laws. Cognitive Science (1981). BACON recovered Kepler’s third law and Ohm’s law from tables of numbers by searching for invariants. The first data-driven discovery program, with no hypothesis in the loop.
Kulkarni and Simon (1988): The Processes of Scientific Discovery: The Strategy of Experimentation. Cognitive Science (1988). KEKADA reproduces Krebs’s path to the urea cycle, built from Holmes’s notebook-based reconstruction; surprise is one of its control signals. The one prior system built the way this seminar proposes to build: from documented human practice.
King et al. (2009): The Automation of Science. Science (2009). The Robot Scientist Adam: a closed generate-and-test loop with a real laboratory, and the first discovery credited to a machine. The best-argued case for the loop. Read it before criticizing the loop.
Schmidt and Lipson (2009): Distilling Free-Form Natural Laws from Experimental Data. Science (2009). Symbolic regression recovers conservation laws from motion-capture data. What “law discovery” means when the variables have already been chosen.

Current systems and their scrutiny.

Wang et al. (2023): Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence. Nature (2023). The standard review. Use it as an index; it is not evidence about any one system.
Kitano (2021): Nobel Turing Challenge: creating the engine for scientific discovery. npj Systems Biology and Applications (2021). The explicit proposal for a closed-loop AI scientist and what it would have to do. The clearest statement of the design this seminar is questioning.
Gottweis et al. (2026): Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist. Nature (2026). The multi-agent hypothesis tournament, now peer reviewed. Compare the validated cases with the number of proposals generated.
Szymanski et al. (2023) and Leeman et al. (2024): An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials, Nature (2023); Challenges in High-Throughput Inorganic Materials Prediction and Autonomous Synthesis, PRX Energy (2024). A closed-loop laboratory reported forty-one new compounds; the reanalysis found most were misidentified or already known. A discovery / scrutiny pair for an autonomous system, and the reason the evaluation protocol has negative controls.
Kapoor and Narayanan (2023): Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science. Patterns (2023). A taxonomy of leakage with cases across fields. Read before reusing any benchmark.
Si et al. (2025), from meeting 10, is the human-baseline study for idea generation.

Objectives other than a hypothesis test.

Rainforth et al. (2024): Modern Bayesian Experimental Design. Statistical Science (2024). Expected information gain as the rule for choosing the next experiment. The strongest formal version of a loop, and it needs a space of models rather than one hypothesis.
Lehman and Stanley (2011): Abandoning Objectives: Evolution Through the Search for Novelty Alone. Evolutionary Computation (2011). Searching for behavioral novelty instead of for an objective solved problems that objective search could not, because the objective was deceptive. The machine-side argument that a gate can narrow the search, stated so it can be tested.
Schmidhuber (2010), from meeting 8, defines interestingness as compression progress, a third candidate objective.

The prior art chapter lists systems and benchmarks that already exist. Consult it before specifying anything here, and record which existing work each part of the architecture builds on.

text:
Reconstruct an inquiry trajectory
These are proposed design instruments, not validated measures of scientific quality. Revise them using the seminar cases. Keep factual support, uncertainty, scientific value, and implementation quality separate. The measurement warning is central: a repeatable score can still measure the wrong thing. (Flake and Fried 2020; Messick 1995)
Use a documented episode, not only the final paper’s rhetorical structure. When the chronology is unknown, mark it as unknown rather than inventing an origin story.
Exercise: compare a proposal’s intended sequence, the work actually performed, and the published narrative. Differences are not automatically misconduct or poor practice; ask which changes were disclosed and what claims remain warranted. Use the methodological contrast in Meeting 1 and the exploratory cases in Meeting 2. (Platt 1964; Cleland 2001, 2002; Steinle 1997; Karaca 2013)

title: Working rubrics and discussion worksheets
text:
Field
What the group records




Initial knowledge and question
What was available before the relevant action? Was there a specific hypothesis?


Action and purpose
Observe, characterize, calibrate, change representation, compare, simulate, test, or synthesize. Why this action now?


Result
The observation or output, including units, uncertainty, missingness, and provenance.


Interpretation
What the result supports, competing interpretations, and assumptions.


Next decision
What changed in the question, instrument, representation, or strategy?


Process evidence
Notebook, dated analysis, paper, interview, retrospective recollection, or an explicitly labeled reconstruction.


Agent requirement
An observable capability, the information it requires, and a test that could reveal failure.

title: Working rubrics and discussion worksheets
text:
Inquiry-mode ledger
One table for the whole quarter, one row per reconstructed episode, filled in during the last five minutes of meetings 1 through 9 and read back in meeting 13. The trajectory worksheet above records one episode in depth; the ledger records what the nine episodes say together. Its point is the two columns on the right: whether a hypothesis gate, meaning a rule that the next action must test a stated hypothesis, would have helped, hurt, or not applied at the decisive step. A ledger in which every row says “hurt” is a finding about how the cases were chosen, not about science, and should be read that way.



Column
What the group records




Episode
The case, and the paper it was reconstructed from.


Decisive move
The action that changed what came next: an observation, a representation, an instrument, a concept, a test, or a synthesis.


Mode
One of the ten in the glossary: observation and description; exploratory discovery; hypothesis testing; theory and mechanistic modeling; simulation and prediction; instruments and observing systems; methods and computation; synthesis and reconstruction; replication and validation; use-inspired and co-produced research. Record a sub-mode where the glossary names one, and flag shared infrastructure.


Known at the start
What was available before the decisive move, and whether a specific hypothesis was among it.


When a hypothesis appeared
Before the decisive move, during it, after it, or never.


A gate would have
Helped, hurt, or not applied, with one sentence of reason.


Evidence basis
Notebook, dated analysis, archive, primary paper, interview, retrospective, or a labelled reconstruction.



The live table is on the meeting notes page, so that each row is signed and dated. Disagree by adding a second row for the same episode rather than editing the first.

title: Working rubrics and discussion worksheets
text:
Novelty Dossier v1
The object of evaluation is an exact contribution claim, not how impressive its abstract sounds. Atypical combinations and semantic distance are possible indicators of particular kinds of novelty, not a complete definition. (Uzzi et al. 2013; Fontana et al. 2020)







Field
Required record




Atomic claim
One observation, method, concept, explanation, connection, or question at a time.


Reference frame
Community, corpus, languages searched, publication cutoff, and search date.


Closest precedent
Specific prior work and the passage or result that overlaps with the claim.


Novel component
What apparently goes beyond that precedent, and which novelty dimension it belongs to.


Attempted falsification
Searches and comparisons designed to find an earlier equivalent, not just supportive citations.


Search limits
Inaccessible texts, older terminology, incomplete indexing, or missing disciplinary coverage.


Judgment
Exact precedent, close precedent, component precedent, apparently new component, or unresolved.


Separate assessments
Correctness, plausibility, feasibility, significance, and expected impact are not the novelty judgment.



Use “no precedent located within this search”, not “never done before”, when the latter cannot be justified. Preserve expert disagreement with its reasons. Human ratings are useful comparators, not infallible labels; actual grant-review research motivates that distinction. (Boudreau et al. 2016)
For an agent test, use a paraphrase of an established result, an established method producing a genuinely new observation, and an apparently new claim with a concealed older precedent. Evaluate prior-art retrieval, localization of the claimed difference, false novelty claims, missed novelty, and appropriate uncertainty. A historical replay is a teaching exercise, not automatically a leakage-free test: withholding later papers from retrieval does not remove them from a model’s training.

title: Working rubrics and discussion worksheets
text:
Scientific Advance Profile v1
Use these working distinctions in discussion rather than treating them as a settled philosophical taxonomy. Novelty is about what is new; innovation about a new way inquiry can be done; advance about a warranted gain in knowledge, understanding, or scientific capability; impact about downstream uptake or consequences. Dellsén offers a position about understanding to argue with, while the Wu-Petersen pairing illustrates the risks of converting citation patterns into a general progress measure. (Dellsén 2016; Wu et al. 2019; Petersen et al. 2025)







Field
Question




Before / after
What could not be known, measured, explained, or tested before the contribution?


Evidence of gain
Which result supports the claimed change? Is it prospective promise or demonstrated gain?


Contribution role
Incremental, corrective, enabling, integrative, transformative, or more than one.


Dependencies
Which instruments, datasets, methods, people, standards, and earlier results made it possible?


Users and consequences
Who could use the result, and what new question, test, or practice would it enable?


Time horizon
What is visible now, what requires later uptake, and what may never be captured by citations?


Uncertainty and disagreement
What evidence would change the assessment?



Exercise: compare a celebrated theoretical paper with a careful calibration, negative result, replication, or curated archive. Hide venue and citation counts initially. Build a contribution-dependency map and distinguish novelty from significance. Consider delayed recognition and changes in who can enter a field, without generalizing a single bibliometric study to all disciplines. (Wang et al. 2017; Azoulay et al. 2019)

title: Working rubrics and discussion worksheets
text:
Agent evaluation protocol v1
A benchmark of tasks reconstructed from papers can evaluate useful analysis capabilities. It does not automatically evaluate selecting a worthwhile research question, detecting an unexpected phenomenon, or changing a field. Define the intended construct before choosing the score. (Chen et al. 2025; Flake and Fried 2020)

Design before running
Use a small set of nonconfidential Earth-science cases. Compare a human baseline, a hypothesis-first agent, and an inquiry-routing agent. Define whether the question concerns architecture, model capability, or end-to-end system utility. To isolate architecture, hold the model and tool access fixed as far as possible; a human comparison needs an explicit account of unequal experience and resources.
Freeze the task packet, data split, permitted information, resource budget, scoring rubric, and stopping rule. Record versions, prompts, code, visible actions, tool outputs, and human interventions. Do not require access to a model’s private internal reasoning; assess its observable behavior, evidence, and reproducible artifacts.


A compact test set







Test
Failure it is intended to expose




Positive control
Failure to recover a known signal or established relation.


Negative control
Confidently inventing structure or causation where the case supplies none.


Measurement artifact
Mistaking a processing or instrument change for a physical discovery.


Missing metadata
Proceeding despite information essential to interpretation.


Paraphrase and irrelevant-variable changes
Sensitivity to wording or irrelevant features rather than the scientific content.


Independent period or region
Failure to generalize beyond the observations used to formulate the claim.


Valuable replication or calibration
Devaluing trustworthy cumulative work because it looks less novel.


Component ablation
A claimed architectural benefit that persists unchanged without the component.



Run a prespecified number of repeated trials within a fixed budget; report every run, not only the best. Separate development cases from held-out assessment cases. Reusing the holdout to tune prompts turns it into development data. Analyze failures and uncertainty before concluding that one system wins.


Report a profile, not an unexamined total score
Report scientific support for the claim, reproducibility, measurement/provenance checks, usefulness of selected actions, handling of alternatives and missing information, novelty judgment, advance profile, and cost. Evaluate confidence calibration across multiple appropriately labeled cases rather than calling one cautious answer “well calibrated.” Use blinded independent assessors where practical, record disagreement, and do not collapse all dimensions into a composite until its interpretation is justified.
Final deliverable: a benchmark specification, the completed test cases, an agent architecture, a failure taxonomy, and a short statement of what the evaluation does and does not establish.

title: Prior art: agents and benchmarks for science
text:
How to read the last column
This chapter exists so that nothing in meeting 13 is specified from scratch. Systems that automate parts of research already exist, and so do benchmarks that score them. Before proposing an architecture or a test, find out whether it has been built, and what happened.
Every entry carries a resolvable identifier, a DOI or an arXiv ID, so the list can be worked through by a person or by a program. Entries were checked against publisher or arXiv records; where a project has multiple versions, the identifier points at the version consulted.
The rightmost column is the point of the chapter. A benchmark score is a measurement, and a measurement supports a claim only about the construct it observes. This is the problem Flake and Fried (2020) and Messick (1995) describe for psychological measures, and it does not change when the thing being measured is an agent. “Solved 40% of the tasks” is a fact about the tasks. Whether it is evidence that a system does science depends entirely on what the tasks required, and most of these task sets deliberately supply the question, the data, and the success criterion. That is to say, they supply most of what meetings 1 through 9 treated as the hard part.
Read that column as an inventory of open problems rather than as criticism. Where a capability the group cares about appears in no existing evaluation, that gap is the group’s opportunity.

Systems that act



Project
What it is
What it covers
What its results do not establish




Coscientist — Boiko et al. (2023)
Language model with web search, documentation retrieval, code execution, and a robotic liquid handler
Planning and executing a chemical synthesis, including optimizing a catalytic cross-coupling on real hardware
That the system chose the question, or that it transfers beyond tasks with existing published protocols and a defined target


The AI Scientist (arXiv:2408.06292) and v2 (arXiv:2504.08066)

Producing complete machine-learning papers without human intervention; v2 reports a workshop-accepted manuscript

Co-Scientist — Gottweis et al. (2026); preprint arXiv:2502.18864
Multi-agent system generating, debating, and ranking hypotheses in a tournament; the peer-reviewed report appeared in Nature in 2026
Proposing biomedical hypotheses, with wet-lab follow-up reported in three areas
General hypothesis quality. The validated cases were selected, and a rate would require the denominator: how many proposals failed


TinyScientist (arXiv:2510.06579)
An open framework for assembling research agents, not a result
Tooling: a controllable, extensible harness others can build on
Anything about scientific performance; it is infrastructure, and belongs here as a starting point rather than as evidence

title: Prior art: agents and benchmarks for science
text:
Systems that predate language models
The tables above start in 2023. Automated discovery did not. The systems below are the record that current ones rarely cite, and one of them was built the way this seminar proposes to build: from a historian’s reconstruction of a scientist’s notebooks. Herbert Simon’s argument that discovery has a describable logic, Simon (1973), is the position all of them assume.









Project
What it is
What it covered
What its results do not establish




BACON — Langley (1981)
Heuristic search for invariants in tables of numeric data
Rediscovered Kepler’s third law, Ohm’s law, and others from the original data
Anything about choosing the variables or the data; both were supplied


KEKADA — Kulkarni and Simon (1988)
A model of Krebs’s discovery of the urea cycle, built from Holmes’s notebook-based reconstruction; surprise and confirmation are explicit control signals
Reproduces the sequence of experiments Krebs ran, including the exploratory phase before any hypothesis
That the strategy transfers to another scientist or problem. It is one episode, modelled after the fact


Robot Scientist Adam — King et al. (2009)
A closed loop: hypothesis generation, experiment selection, robotic execution, and analysis, in yeast functional genomics
The first discovery attributed to a machine, later confirmed by hand
That the loop generalizes beyond a domain with an enumerable hypothesis space and a fully automated assay


Eureqa — Schmidt and Lipson (2009)
Symbolic regression over experimental time series
Recovered Lagrangians and Hamiltonians for pendulums and oscillators
Which variables to measure; the search space is fixed by the input columns


Literature-based discovery — Swanson (1986)
Connecting two literatures that never cite each other, first done by reading and later by program
The fish-oil and Raynaud’s syndrome link, later confirmed clinically
How often the method produces false connections. The successes are what got reported



Two more belong in the record as arguments rather than systems. Kitano (2021) states the closed-loop AI-scientist design explicitly and lists what it would have to do. Wang et al. (2023) is the standard review of the field since; use it as an index, not as evidence.

Benchmarks and evaluations



Project
What it is
What it covers
What its scores do not establish




ScienceAgentBench — Chen et al. (2025)
102 executable tasks drawn from 44 peer-reviewed papers, validated by subject-matter experts
Data-driven analysis: given a question and data, produce working code and the right output
Question formation, novelty, or discovery. The task supplies what earlier meetings identified as the difficult and interesting choices


DiscoveryBench (ICLR 2025; preprint arXiv:2407.01725)
264 tasks derived from published papers, each a multi-step search for a stated relationship in supplied data, plus 903 synthetic tasks
Data-driven discovery as a workflow: the system must find the relationship, not only run an analysis. The best system reported scored 25%
Question formation: the goal is stated in words for every task, and the data are supplied. Transfer beyond the six domains covered is untested


MLE-bench (ICLR 2025; preprint arXiv:2410.07095)
75 Kaggle competitions run as machine-learning engineering tasks
Engineering competence: building a model that scores well against a defined metric
Any scientific claim. A Kaggle task arrives with the target, the metric, and the guarantee that a solution exists


Gravity-Bench-v1 (ICML 2025; preprint arXiv:2501.18411)
Simulated gravitational systems where the agent must plan its own observations
Closer to inquiry than most: the agent decides what to measure, under a budget, including out-of-distribution physics
Performance with real instruments, real noise, real calibration, or a real literature to be wrong about


LLM-SRBench (ICML 2025; preprint arXiv:2504.10415)
Equation-discovery tasks built to resist recall of known formulas
Whether a system can find a governing relation in data rather than retrieve one it has seen
Inquiry beyond the symbolic-regression step. The data, the variables, and the goal are given


FML-bench (arXiv:2510.10472)
Machine-learning research tasks scored on multiple axes
Broader research behavior than single-task benchmarks
Transfer outside machine learning, which is the field these agents were largely trained on


Human study of LLM ideation — Si et al. (2025)
A blinded comparison of research ideas written by over a hundred NLP researchers and by a language-model agent, judged by expert reviewers
Novelty, excitement, and feasibility of the ideas themselves; the model’s ideas rated higher on novelty and lower on feasibility
That a novel-rated idea leads to good work. Execution is a separate study, and the field is NLP


NovBench — Wu et al. (2026)
Evaluation of model judgments of paper novelty
Whether a model’s novelty assessment agrees with expert assessment on NLP papers
That the judgments transfer to Earth science. Whether they do is itself something to check. See meeting 10

title: Prior art: agents and benchmarks for science
section: What is missing from all of them
text:
What is missing from all of them
Collecting the last columns gives the group a short list of capabilities that appear in no evaluation above:

Choosing the question. Every benchmark supplies it. Meetings 1, 2, and 6 treated question formation as the substance of inquiry.
Deciding what to measure, and whether the measurement can be trusted. Only Gravity-Bench asks an agent to plan observations, and it does so in simulation with no instrument response. Compare the provenance concerns in meeting 5.
Reasoning from traces of the past. Nothing here evaluates inference about events that cannot be re-run, which is the mode of meeting 3 and much of this group’s science.
Recognizing a surprise worth following. Anomaly detection appears; judging an anomaly interesting does not. See meeting 8.
Abstaining. No benchmark rewards a system for concluding that the evidence is insufficient, though meeting 9 treats that as a competent outcome.
Field and marine constraint. Ship time, weather, instrument loss, and the plan-versus-reality gap of meeting 7 have no representation at all.
Effects on the field. Hao et al. (2026) measured, across 41 million papers, that scientists who use AI tools publish more and that the fields they work in narrow. No benchmark scores a system on what it does to the questions a field asks. See meeting 11 and Messeri and Crockett (2024).

These seven are the natural content of the benchmark drafted in meeting 13. Whether any of them can be measured well is itself uncertain, and a benchmark the group cannot actually run is not an improvement over one that exists.

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
Questions
The seminar reconstructs nine episodes by hand. This page designs the counterpart at scale: code the mode of inquiry of published papers, measure their impact, novelty, interdisciplinarity, and depth, and ask which modes dominate the literature, which dominate the papers that shaped a field, and how mode and impact relate. It is a design, with a feasibility check, not a result. The group decides in meeting 1 whether to run it, and the timeline below is keyed to meetings rather than dates.
Every citation links to its full record in the bibliography. The glossary is the codebook. The definitions there were written before any paper was coded, and the analysis plan below is meant to be frozen before the coding starts, so that the group practises the distinction meeting 6 is about (Nosek et al. 2018) rather than only reading about it.
The fourth question is the one the seminar is best placed to answer and the literature cannot: it needs notebooks, retrospectives, and people in the room.
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
What share of papers in a field presents each mode of inquiry as its decisive move, and how has that share changed since 1970?
Among field-shaping papers, defined below, is the distribution of modes different from the field’s baseline?
How does a paper’s mode relate to its impact, its novelty, its interdisciplinarity, and its depth, holding year and subfield fixed?
Where a trajectory is documented, does the presented mode match the reconstructed one, and does the mismatch depend on impact?
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
What is already measured
Research strategies have been coded at scale for biomedicine, where most work is conservative, innovative work is rare and rewarded more, and careers set the balance (Foster et al. 2015). Novelty as atypical combination predicts high impact when paired with a conventional core (Uzzi et al. 2013), and interdisciplinarity has a measured cost in output and a measured reward in citations (Leahey et al. 2017). Disruption has been measured across the whole literature and found to decline (Park et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2019), and the measure has been shown to inflate with the growth of reference lists (Petersen et al. 2025). Fields that grow large entrench their canon (Chu and Evans 2021).
What has not been measured, as far as the reading for this seminar has found, is the share of modes of inquiry in a literature, coded from the papers themselves against a stated taxonomy, and its relation to those outcomes. The nearest work is the debate over hypothesis-driven versus data-driven biology, which argued the question from cases rather than counts (Kell and Oliver 2004; Glass and Hall 2008), and a survey of what ecologists count as good science in a data-rich field (Elliott et al. 2016). Step 0 of the study is a proper search for prior work of this kind, recorded in the Novelty Dossier format, before anything is coded.
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
Units and corpus
The unit is the paper. The source is OpenAlex, which is open, has an API, and supplies for each work its abstract where the publisher allows, its references, its citing works, topic assignments, and a citation percentile normalized by field and year.
The home corpus is seismology, this group’s field, so that the group can judge the coding. A feasibility query on September 6, 2026 found about 22,000 journal articles from 1970 to 2020 under OpenAlex’s seismology topic, about 10,000 of them with an abstract, and about 290 cited more than a hundred times. Topic assignment is noisy, so the working definition of the corpus should be a journal set, for example the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, Geophysical Journal International, Seismological Research Letters, and the seismology papers in Geophysical Research Letters and Nature Geoscience, rather than a topic label. A comparison corpus from a field Platt held up as fast, molecular biology, tests whether the mode shares are a property of the field or of science.
Abstracts are enough for a first pass and are wrong often enough that the pilot codes full texts. The published abstract is the narrative at its most compressed.
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
Coding scheme
Each paper is coded for:

Decisive mode, one of the ten in the glossary, as presented by the paper.
Sub-mode, where the glossary names one.
Secondary modes, any number.
Hypothesis stated before the result, as presented: yes, no, or cannot tell. This is the variable the seminar’s thesis is about, separate from the mode.
Intervention on the system: yes or no.
New instrument or method as the contribution: yes or no.
New data collected: yes, reused, or none.
Shared infrastructure: yes or no, for a network, a dataset or catalog, a software package, or a standard offered for others’ use.
Coder confidence, three levels, and one sentence of reason.

A coder sees the title, abstract, and full text, and does not see the journal, the authors, the year, or the citation count. Blinding matters here more than usual, because the convenor’s thesis is known to everyone coding, and because prestige cues are exactly what a classifier would learn from if they were left in (Kapoor and Narayanan 2023).
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
Procedure
Pilot. One hundred papers drawn at random from the home corpus, coded independently by two people, agreement reported per variable with a chance-corrected statistic, and every disagreement discussed and recorded. The glossary is revised where the disagreements show a definition failing. This is the meeting 6 case exercise if the group wants it to be.
Classifier. A language-model classifier given the revised glossary as its instructions, applied to a further three hundred papers that two people have coded and that the classifier has not seen. Report precision and recall per mode, and the confusion between modes, not an overall accuracy; a classifier that is right about hypothesis testing and wrong about synthesis and reconstruction is useless for this question. Treat the classifier as a measurement instrument, which means asking what construct its scores observe before using them (Flake and Fried 2020). Keep the human-coded set as the standard and re-check the classifier on a fresh sample each time the glossary changes.
Scale. The classifier applied to the full corpus, with the coder-confidence variable kept and low-confidence papers sampled for human review.
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
Measures
Impact. Citation percentile normalized by field and year, which OpenAlex supplies and which follows the universal form found across fields (Radicchi et al. 2008); top 1% and top 10% as strata; the choice of indicator justified against the review of what each measures (Waltman 2016). Citation counts are attention as well as use (Bornmann and Daniel 2008), so where the group can, add uptake that citations miss: data and catalogue reuse, and adoption of a method by named later papers.
Field-shaping. Three operationalizations, reported separately, because they do not agree with one another: the disruption index computed from the OpenAlex citation graph (Funk and Owen-Smith 2017; Wu et al. 2019), with the correction for citation inflation (Petersen et al. 2025); canonical status, meaning a paper in the top of its field’s citation distribution that continues to be cited a decade or more after publication (Chu and Evans 2021); and delayed recognition, the sleeping beauty (Ke et al. 2015). A paper that scores on all three is field-shaping on any definition; the interesting cases are the ones that score on one.
Novelty. Atypicality of the paper’s pairs of cited journals against the field’s expectation (Uzzi et al. 2013), and distance of its abstract from the prior literature by word embedding (Shibayama et al. 2021), with the known problems of both recorded (Fontana et al. 2020).
Interdisciplinarity. Diversity of the fields the paper cites, counting variety, balance, and disparity together (Stirling 2007), with OpenAlex fields as the taxonomy and the choice of taxonomy recorded as a limitation (Porter and Rafols 2009; Wagner et al. 2011).
Depth. For the paper, the concentration of its references in one field, the low end of the diversity above. For the first author, the concentration of prior publications across topics (Teodoridis 2018).

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
section: Analysis plan, to be frozen before coding
text:
Analysis plan, to be frozen before coding

Mode shares in the home corpus with confidence intervals, by decade. Question 1.
Mode shares in each field-shaping stratum against a random sample matched on year and subfield. Question 2. Report the three strata separately, and keep instruments and methods apart: the citation habit of tools suggests that method papers are overrepresented among the most cited, and the split exists to test that.
A model of impact percentile on mode, with year and subfield as controls and novelty, interdisciplinarity, and depth as covariates, and the same model with the hypothesis-stated variable in place of mode. Question 3. The second model is the direct test of the seminar’s thesis at the level of narrative.
For the seminar’s own thirty reconstructed episodes, presented mode against reconstructed mode, and the gap against impact. Question 4.
Everything else is exploratory and is labelled so in the write-up (Tukey 1962).
crumbs: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design

title: Which modes dominate the literature? A study design
text:
What can go wrong
The paper reports the presented mode, and standing question 5 says that is not the trajectory. Abstracts follow journal templates, and Platt’s touchstone has been funders’ policy for sixty years (Platt 1964), so a rise in “hypothesis stated” over time may measure the narrative, not the work. Question 4 is the only control on this, and it is small.
The corpus is what was published, so modes that fail before publication are invisible, which is the selection problem the seminar sees in Burke and in Moore.
Mode is not quality. A field-shaping paper in one mode may be field-shaping because of the problem, the timing, or the author, not the mode. The regression controls for what can be measured, and the case reconstructions are where the rest lives.
The classifier reads the same literature the field wrote, and its errors will be correlated with the field’s own conventions. Human coding of a held-out set, repeated after each revision, is the only check.
“Field-shaping” is three constructs, not one, and the study reports all three because reducing them to one would be the mistake meeting 12 is about.

title: How to contribute
text:
What must never be published here
This book is the group’s shared workspace, not a finished text. Notes, readings, corrections, and disagreements are all welcome. Everything below is also in CONTRIBUTING.md at the repository root, which is what GitHub shows when you open a pull request.
The repository is public. Before committing anything, check that it contains none of the following.
If you are unsure, ask before committing rather than after. A commit that reaches the public history is not fully undone by a later deletion.

title: How to contribute
text:
Journal PDFs or article full texts. This book distributes links and bibliographic metadata only. Publishers’ terms are not waived by course use. Put reading copies in private/pdfs/, which is ignored by git.
Unpublished data or results, yours or a collaborator’s, including figures from work in review.
Anything a collaborator, student, or reviewer has not agreed to make public. The case exercises ask people to describe how their own projects really went, which is exactly the material that should stay in the private group notes.
Anything from private/. That directory holds the parallel analysis and is excluded by .gitignore; tools/validate.py fails if the ignore rule is missing or if private material is registered as a chapter. Do not defeat either guard.

title: How to contribute
text:
Adding a meeting note
Open meeting notes, find your meeting, and add a signed, dated entry. The “Edit this page” link in the right-hand margin opens the file on GitHub and turns your edit into a pull request without a local clone.
Do not edit someone else’s entry. If you disagree, add your own beneath it and say so. The record is more useful for keeping the disagreement than for resolving it.

title: How to contribute
text:
Adding a reading
Two files are the sources of truth, and they change together:

Append a BibTeX record to references.bib. Give it a key of the form author plus year, a DOI verified against Crossref, and a url that resolves.
Add the matching entry to the references object in curriculum.json: author, year, title, journal, DOI, volume, issue, pages, URL, and an access note.

Then decide where it belongs. A suggestion for the group goes as a bullet in the bibliography, citing the key, with one sentence on the claim and one on the meeting it bears on. An optional extension for a meeting goes in that meeting’s optional list in curriculum.json and as a cited bullet on the session page, with a sentence or two on why it is there. In either case run tools/build_bibliography.py, which regenerates the reading lists on the bibliography page from curriculum.json; tools/validate.py fails if those lists are stale, if the BibTeX keys and the metadata disagree, or if an optional key is not cited on its session page.

title: How to contribute
text:
Adding a prior-art entry
Prior art catalogues systems and benchmarks rather than readings, so it takes a table row rather than a bibliography entry. Include a resolvable DOI or arXiv ID and fill in the last column honestly: what the project’s numbers do not establish. An entry that overstates a limitation is as much a problem as one that omits it. Say so in the pull request if you have actually run the system.

title: How to contribute
text:
Changing the curriculum
Session pages and curriculum.json hold the same prose, and tools/validate.py checks that the assigned citation keys agree. Change both together. There are thirteen meetings, numbered in order; they are taken one at a time and carry no dates.
Substantive changes to what is assigned should start as an issue, and the rationale belongs in READING-AUDIT.md alongside the existing entries.

section: Checking your work before you push
text:
Checking your work before you push
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install PyYAML
.venv/bin/python tools/validate.py
quarto render
A virtual environment rather than a plain pip install because recent macOS and Linux Pythons refuse to install into the system interpreter. .venv/ is gitignored.
validate.py checks chapter existence, local links, citation keys, the schedule, the agreement between references.bib and curriculum.json, and that the generated reading lists in bibliography.qmd are current, then runs a Pandoc citation pass that fails on any warning. The same checks run on every pull request.
If you changed a reference or added a prior-art entry, also run .venv/bin/python tools/check_links.py. It verifies every DOI against Crossref and fetches every other URL. A handful of publisher sites answer automated requests with 403; the script reports those separately and does not treat them as failures.

title: How to contribute
text:
Style
Match the surrounding pages. The book states what a source does and does not establish, labels reconstruction as inference, and avoids treating a first-person account, a philosophical argument, and a controlled study as interchangeable evidence. Keep claims proportionate to what was actually shown, and prefer “no precedent located within this search” to “never done before”.

title: Bibliography and reading library
text:
By meeting
One page for every reading in the book. The first part is organized for use: the papers assigned to each meeting, the discussant-led papers, and the optional extensions, each with an official link and an access note. The last part is the formal reference list, generated from references.bib; every citation anywhere in the book links to its entry there. Readings the group adds during the quarter go in their own section. Systems and benchmarks are catalogued in prior art, because they are software and evaluations rather than readings.
Use official links rather than uploaded copies. Access notes distinguish a publisher record from an identified free full-text route; institutional entitlement is not guaranteed. This book distributes links and bibliographic metadata only, and no journal PDF is redistributed here.
The reading lists below are generated by tools/build_bibliography.py from references.bib and curriculum.json, and tools/validate.py fails if they are out of date. Edit the sources and rerun the script rather than editing the lists by hand.
